strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: inference-time safety alignment for LALMs, where prior work has focused almost exclusively on LLMs/LVLMs.

Strong motivating analysis: the paper convincingly demonstrates via t-SNE visualization that harmful/safe audio activations remain persistently separated across all layers (unlike text, where separability emerges only at intermediate depths), providing a clear mechanistic explanation for why vanilla activation steering transferred from LLMs fails on audio inputs.

Introduces the Balanced Refusal Rate (BRR) metric and constructs paired harmful-safe audio datasets (Figstep-audio, AdvBench-audio) that expose over-refusal on borderline-safe queries -- a gap that existing benign-only benchmarks miss; this is a useful methodological contribution independent of the main method.

The proposed method (text-derived refusal steering + PCA-based decomposed safe-space ablation) is simple, well-motivated by the preceding empirical analysis, and computationally lightweight (training-free, inference-time only).

Extensive empirical validation: results span four harmfulness benchmarks, two helpfulness benchmarks, one general-utility benchmark, two different LALM backbones (Qwen2-Audio, Kimi-Audio), with consistent improvements over multiple baselines (AdaShield, FSD, MDSteer-h2s/c2r).

Thorough ablation and sensitivity analyses (component ablation V1/V2/V3, sample number n, scaling coefficient alpha, PCA rank k) plus supplementary studies (refusal direction choice, refusal prompt choice, base-model results, generalization to text-only LLMs) that substantially strengthen the empirical case and reproducibility.

A mathematical intuition (local linearization argument) is provided to explain why the ablation should behave differently for harmful, regular-safe, and borderline-safe inputs, adding some theoretical grounding beyond pure empiricism.
weaknesses: Dataset construction relies heavily on LLM-based paraphrasing (DeepSeek-R1) to generate 'safe' counterparts to harmful queries, TTS synthesis, and a single fixed unifying instruction template; there is no human verification/quality-control step reported for these synthetic paired datasets, which are central to both the analysis and the method's calibration (PCA subspace, refusal vector).

Only two LALM backbones are evaluated (Qwen2-Audio, Kimi-Audio); broader coverage of architectures (e.g., SALMONN, MiDashengLM, VITA-Audio) would strengthen claims of generality given the paper explicitly argues audio-modality behavior is architecture/encoder dependent.

No fine-tuning-based baseline is included for comparison, even though the introduction motivates inference-time defenses partly as an alternative to costly fine-tuning; without at least one SFT/RLHF-style safety-tuned reference, it's hard to gauge how much headroom remains relative to a stronger (if costlier) alternative.

The BRR metric uses a fixed 1/2-1/2 weighting between harmful-refusal and safe-non-refusal with no sensitivity analysis or justification for this choice, and as an averaged metric it can mask cases where one sub-term is poor (e.g., MDSteer-c2r's BRR on AdvBench-audio appears competitive despite very high ASR elsewhere).

Evaluation relies on automated judges only (matching-based keyword list in Table 4 and an LLM-based Mistral-7b judge); no human evaluation or inter-annotator agreement is reported to validate these automated metrics, and the keyword-matching refusal detector is fairly coarse and could misclassify nuanced or partial refusals.

Baseline comparisons are limited to two prompt-based (AdaShield, FSD) and two steering-based (MDSteer-h2s/c2r) methods adapted from other modalities; more recent hidden-state-based multimodal defenses (e.g., HiddenDetect, ETA) are discussed in related work but not empirically adapted and compared, leaving open whether SARSteer's advantage would persist against stronger detection-based competitors.

Hyperparameters (alpha=0.1, k=10) appear tuned specifically for the tested models/datasets; while sensitivity plots show relative robustness within the tested range, no principled method for selecting them on a new model/dataset combination is provided beyond grid search.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuinely underexplored problem (inference-time safety alignment for LALMs) and provides a clear, evidence-based motivation via two empirical studies (Section 3.3 t-SNE analysis showing audio harmful/safe representations are persistently separated unlike text, and Section 3.4 quantifying over-refusal of transferred LVLM prompt defenses).

Construction of paired harmful-safe audio datasets (Figstep-audio, AdvBench-audio, SORRY-Bench-audio) is a useful artifact that fills a gap in existing benign-only benchmarks and enables a sharper evaluation of the safety-helpfulness trade-off via the introduced Balanced Refusal Rate (BRR) metric.

The proposed method (text-derived refusal steering + PCA-based safe-subspace ablation) is simple, interpretable, and directly motivated by the diagnosed failure modes, with an accompanying (if approximate) mathematical justification (Appendix A.4).

Reasonably extensive experiments: two LALMs, four harmfulness benchmarks, two paired helpfulness benchmarks, general-utility benchmark, ablations on components, and sensitivity analysis over n, alpha, and k, plus base-model and text-LLM generalization checks.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is modest: both core ingredients (difference-in-means/refusal-direction steering and PCA-based subspace removal) are adapted fairly directly from prior LLM/LVLM literature (Arditi et al., Zhao et al., Panickssery et al.); the contribution is largely the application/combination to a new modality rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The 'text-derived' steering vector is still computed using 100 harmful audio-paired samples (Qs_harm) to obtain mu_harm and mu_harm-tr, so the method is not as audio-agnostic as claimed — it still depends on curated harmful audio queries, only avoiding an audio-to-audio contrastive pair.

Evaluation is limited to only two open-source LALMs (Qwen2-Audio, Kimi-Audio); no larger or more recent/capable models are tested, limiting confidence in generalizability of the findings, especially the audio-representation separability claim that underlies the entire motivation.

Baseline behavior is highly inconsistent across models (e.g., AdaShield ASR goes from 0.00% on Kimi-Audio to 30.00% on Qwen2-Audio in Table 2, and FSD's effect flips direction between models), which is only superficially explained by 'model-specific behavior' without deeper investigation — this raises concerns about whether baselines are optimally/fairly implemented and adapted.

The safe-query paraphrasing pipeline relies on an LLM (DeepSeek-R1) to generate lexically-similar 'purified' benign queries, but there is no human verification or quality/safety check of these generated pairs, so the paired dataset's reliability (a load-bearing element for all main claims) is not independently validated.

Robustness to adaptive/optimized audio jailbreaks (e.g., adversarial perturbations as in AJailBench) is only lightly evaluated (200 sampled queries, single ASR number) without deeper analysis of whether SARSteer's steering vector could be circumvented by an adaptive attacker aware of the defense.

The mathematical justification in Appendix A.4 relies on a first-order local linearization assumption and offers only qualitative intuition (signs of inner products) rather than a rigorous bound, and does not address why the PCA safe-subspace should generalize to held-out or entirely different types of benign queries beyond the specific paired dataset used to fit it.

Computational/latency overhead of layer-wise activation intervention at every generation step, and any need to recompute vectors per model/dataset, is not discussed, which matters for the claimed 'scalable deployment' advantage over fine-tuning.

strengths: Identifies and clearly motivates a previously underexplored problem: safety alignment for LALMs, with well-designed diagnostic experiments (t-SNE analysis) convincingly showing why LLM-style activation steering fails when computed directly from audio inputs due to persistent modality-specific separation between harmful/safe representations.

Proposes a simple, principled, and computationally cheap two-part method (text-derived refusal steering + PCA-based safe-subspace ablation) that directly targets the two identified failure modes (audio steering failure and prompt-based over-refusal), and provides a plausible linearized theoretical justification for why it should work differently on harmful/regular-safe/borderline-safe inputs.

Introduces a useful new evaluation protocol/metric (paired harmful-safe datasets and Balanced Refusal Rate) that specifically targets the previously under-measured over-refusal phenomenon, filling a genuine gap in existing benign-only benchmarks.

Extensive empirical evaluation across two LALMs (Qwen2-Audio, Kimi-Audio), four harmfulness benchmarks, two paired helpfulness benchmarks, and a general-utility benchmark, with consistent improvements over multiple reasonable baselines (AdaShield, FSD, MDSteer variants).

Thorough ablation studies (component ablation, sample size, scaling coefficient, PCA rank, refusal-direction choice, refusal-prompt choice, base-model performance, and even generalization to text-only LLMs), which strengthen confidence that the reported gains are not fragile or cherry-picked.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to only two open-source LALMs; broader claims about generality of the audio-steering failure and of SARSteer's effectiveness would benefit from testing on additional/newer architectures (e.g., end-to-end speech LLMs with different audio encoders).

The constructed datasets (Figstep-audio, AdvBench-audio, SORRY-Bench-audio, and the LLM-purified 'safe' counterparts) are synthesized via TTS and DeepSeek-R1 purification without reported human quality checks, so there is a risk that dataset artifacts (e.g., TTS pronunciation issues, imperfect purification changing intended semantics) partly drive both the motivating failure analyses and the main results.

No evaluation against adaptive or steering-aware jailbreak attacks; all harmfulness benchmarks are static and non-adaptive, so the paper cannot demonstrate robustness to an adversary that is aware of the SARSteer mechanism and tries to circumvent it (e.g., via adversarial audio perturbations targeting the steering direction).

Evaluation relies heavily on an LLM-as-judge (Mistral-7B fine-tuned for SORRY-Bench) and keyword-matching for refusal detection; no inter-annotator or human-validation check is reported to confirm the reliability of ASR/RR judgments, which is important given how central these metrics are to all claims.

The 'mathematical intuition' in Appendix A.4 relies on a first-order local linearization of the refusal logit and informal assumptions about subspace alignment; it offers plausibility rather than a rigorous guarantee, and is not empirically validated (e.g., by directly measuring w^T v_perp on real activations).

No comparison to any fine-tuning-based safety defenses (even as a lightweight upper-bound reference) is provided, making it hard to gauge how much performance is sacrificed for the practicality of an inference-time-only method.

The hyperparameter α is tuned per setting via sweep (Figure 5b) but the paper does not clearly specify a principled or automatic way to select α at deployment time, which could affect reproducibility/practicality across new domains or models.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and important problem: inference-time safety alignment for Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs), where audio has been shown to be more jailbreak-prone than text.

Strong diagnostic analysis in Section 3: t-SNE visualizations and (in the appendix) quantitative CKA measurements convincingly show why naively transferred LLM-style activation steering fails on audio inputs (harmful/safe audio representations are already separated at all layers, unlike text).

The proposed two-stage method (text-derived refusal steering + PCA-based decomposed safe-space ablation) is simple, well-motivated by the preceding failure analysis, and accompanied by a first-order mathematical argument (Appendix A.4) explaining why it should selectively affect harmful but not safe/borderline-safe activations.

Construction of paired harmful-safe audio datasets (Figstep-audio, AdvBench-audio, SORRY-Bench-audio) is a useful methodological contribution that enables a sharper, previously missing evaluation of over-refusal via the introduced Balanced Refusal Rate (BRR) metric.

Extensive main and appendix experiments: multiple LALMs (Qwen2-Audio, Kimi-Audio, plus MiDashengLM, Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni, Voxtral in the appendix), multiple harmfulness benchmarks, general-utility evaluation on AirBench, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, ablations isolating each component, comparison to a fine-tuning baseline (RRS), robustness to adversarial/signal perturbations and adaptive attacks (PGD, Gaussian noise, audio-adapted PAIR/GCG), and a human evaluation of the LLM-judge protocol (κ=0.811) that helps validate the ASR metric and characterizes its conservative bias.
The method is inference-time only (no fine-tuning), making it practical and efficient (much lower runtime than the RRS fine-tuning baseline).
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core techniques (mean-difference activation steering, PCA-based subspace removal) are established tools from LLM/LVLM interpretability and safety literature; the contribution is largely in identifying the right way to combine/apply them to the audio modality rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Results are not uniformly dominant: in Table 2, AdaShield/FSD sometimes achieve lower ASR than SARSteer (e.g., FSD on Qwen2-Audio Figstep-audio and SORRY-Bench, AdaShield on nearly all Kimi-Audio harmfulness columns), and in the appendix extension to newer models (Table 14), SARSteer is often not the best on ASR (e.g., Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, Voxtral-Mini-3B) though it retains a better BRR/Safe-RR trade-off — the paper's framing as consistently superior slightly overstates this.

The single scalar coefficient α and fixed k are applied uniformly across all layers/models with limited justification for why this generalizes; while sensitivity analysis is shown, only one model (Qwen2-Audio) is used for the α sweep in the main text.

The refusal-rate evaluation relies partly on keyword/phrase matching (Appendix A.6), which is a coarse proxy for actual harmful compliance; although the paper also uses an LLM judge, the human evaluation in Appendix B.11 itself reveals a nontrivial 43/500 disagreement rate, suggesting the reported ASR values (and hence method comparisons) carry non-negligible measurement uncertainty, even if the bias direction is characterized as conservative.

The PCA-based safe-subspace ablation is a linear approximation of the benign semantic manifold; kernel PCA is shown to fail badly (Table 10), and it's unclear whether the linear subspace assumption will hold as the benign query distribution becomes more diverse than the closely lexically-matched paired dataset used for extraction.

Steering vectors and PCA subspaces are derived from a single, relatively narrow source (100 pairs from Figstep-audio) for all downstream evaluation and models; while generalization is empirically demonstrated, the dependence on this specific harmful-safe construction methodology (TTS-converted AdvBench/Figstep style queries with a fixed instruction template) limits confidence that findings transfer to more naturalistic or adversarially diverse harmful audio queries.
